newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia to voice opposition at a US sanctions law.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia to voice opposition at a US sanctions law.

text.p: Malaysia, whose state oil company faces U.S. sanctions for investing in Iran, will challenge Washington's threat in international forums, a senior minister was quoted as saying on Friday.

The country will make its stand at both the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation and World Trade Organisation meetings to be held later this year, the Business Times newspaper quoted International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz as saying.
The newspaper quoted the minister as saying that the United States does not have extra-territorial jurisdiction to impose its laws on other countries.

"We regret that the U.S. has taken steps to act against third countries which are operating in countries in which it has a negative stand," Rafidah told reporters after an official function in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Thursday that Malaysia intends to proceed with a deal to buy a stake in two Iranian oil fields despite the sanctions threat.
"We will go on (with the deal)," Mahathir told reporters. "We are a sovereign nation. We will not submit to what the U.S. dictates to us."

In London on Tuesday, a legislative aide to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato -- the sanctions law's major congressional sponsor -- referred to possible moves against Malaysia's state oil company Petronas, due to its involvement in an Iranian petrochemical project.

But U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary suggested in New York on the same day that the Clinton administration would wait until after the November 5 U.S. elections to decide on how it will enforce its sanctions law against Libya and Iran.
Petronas has a 30 percent stake in Iran's Sirri oilfields exploration project, which also involves French company Total SA.
The investment in the $600 million project puts Petronas over the $40 million a year level that the U.S. has said non-U.S. firms can invest in Iran and Libya's oil and gas sectors.
Rafidah said: "This is not a Petronas issue. It is a matter of principle. The U.S. does not have extra-territorial jurisdiction on other countries."
